title: Birbal and the Fakir
summary: A mendicant asks Akbar for money to build a grand hermitage. Birbal shows the holy man that asking an emperor for gold is merely asking one beggar from another.
full_text:
A famous traveling fakir arrived at the imperial palace of Fatehpur Sikri, requesting an audience with Emperor Akbar. The fakir claimed to have renounced all worldly desires, yet he presented a long petition requesting twenty thousand gold mohurs from the imperial treasury to construct an opulent marble hermitage with fountains and orchards.

Akbar was performing his morning prayers in the private mosque. The fakir was ushered into the anteroom and asked to wait.

Through the arched doorway, the fakir saw Emperor Akbar kneeling upon his prayer mat, with hands raised toward heaven, praying aloud:

'O Almighty Creator! Bestow health upon my children, grant prosperity to my empire, protect my armies, and increase my treasury with wealth and blessing!'

Hearing the Emperor's prayer, the fakir quietly turned around, picked up his walking staff, and began walking toward the palace exit.

Akbar completed his prayers, stepped out into the courtyard, and saw the holy man departing. Akbar called out: 'Holy father! You came to request an imperial grant! Why are you leaving without asking for your gold?'

The fakir replied with quiet dignity:

'Your Majesty, I saw you upon your knees begging the Almighty for more wealth, health, and power.

'I thought you were a rich emperor who had treasures to give. But I see that you are merely a grand beggar, pleading before the King of Kings for your daily bread!

'If I must beg for assistance, why should I beg from a fellow beggar who is himself begging for more? It is far more honorable for me to bring my petition directly to the Almighty Creator who provides for all!'

Akbar was stunned into silence. Birbal stepped forward, bowed low to the fakir, and said to the Emperor:

'Sire, this holy man has delivered the greatest sermon ever spoken in this palace. All mortals, whether clothed in rags or crowned in diamonds, are equal paupers before the throne of the Divine. True dignity lies in relying upon providence and honest labor, not upon royal favor.'

Akbar bowed in deep reverence to the fakir, offered him food, and thanked him for the humbling reminder.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Birbal and the Fakir"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
